2.text: In the Kolyma country the Reindeer Chukchee, like other inhabitants, are

3.text: very assiduous in digging out the young of the white fox, though their skin

4.text: has hardly any value; and this imprudent extermination has already decreased

5.text: the number of foxes. In trade, seven qualities of white-fox skin are distinguished,
5.note: Stray ink speck before initial 'the'; not type. class: artifact.

6.text: according to age; and the first three are valued at not more than from ten

7.text: to fifteen cents apiece. In the Kolyma country the Russianized Yukaghir and

8.text: the Yakut often capture the young of the red fox, and raise them in willow

9.text: baskets or wooden cases. The animals are half starved, because, if well fed,

10.text: they would have thin and uneven fur. They are generally killed early in the

11.text: fall. The Chukchee are too indolent to go to the trouble of raising young

12.text: foxes in this way, and, moreover, they consider it as tabooed. In the
12.note: Two ink specks between 'In' and 'the' (raised comma-like and apostrophe-like marks); not type, same speckling seen elsewhere on this page (L5, L16, L27). class: artifact.

13.text: eastern part of their territory, the Chukchee consider it unfair “to break into

14.text: the house of any resident, even if it be a fox,” because every resident, though

15.text: but a fox, is supposed to have a drum and charms in his house, and vengeance

16.text: through magic means might ensue. Thus only a fox hunted down in the
16.note: Ink speck before 'magic' resembling an apostrophe; not type, same page-wide speckling as L5/L12/L27. class: artifact.

17.text: burrow is dug after, especially since often it does not hide in its own hole.

18.text: TRAPS. — Traps with a spring of twisted sinew (Fig. 48), of the shape
18.note: Run-in heading 'Traps.' is set in small capitals (second-level heading); keyed as plain ASCII capitals per keying_spec.md §2.13.

19.text: common throughout the northern part of the Old World and possibly brought

20.text: thither by the Russians, were much used in northeastern Asia, and even came

21.text: to America; ¹ but on the Pacific they are at present superseded by steel traps
21.note: Footnote reference marker keyed as superscript U+00B9 per keying_spec.md §2.10, not ASCII '1'.

22.text: bought from the whalers, while on the Kolyma and along the Arctic shore

23.text: the sinew-twisted trap still prevails. This trap strikes the animal from above;

24.text: and the blow, though prompt and strong, is not quite sure, since the fox is

25.text: often quick enough to dodge away in time. Then, instead of being killed,

26.text: it is only hurt, and may be able to escape, breaking the trap, or biting through

27.text: the sinew cords. On the other hand, this kind of trap is not very safe for
27.note: Ink speck above 'On'; not type, same page-wide speckling as L5/L12/L16. class: artifact.

28.text: ¹ For description, see Nelson, pp. 122, 123.
